caseno:
Writ Petition No. 4336 of 1996
With
Writ Petition No. 4337 of 1996
lawyer:
Dr. Kamal Hossain with Mr. Abdul Baset Majumder, Mr. Zainul Abedin and Mr. Zakir Hossain Munshi, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner
Mr. K.S. Nabi, Attorney General ------ For Respondent No. 4 
Mr. Zakir Ahmed with Mr. Oziullah, Mr. Iqbal Ahsan Chowdhury and Mr. A.K.M. Enayet Ullah Chowdhury, Advocates ------ For Respondent No. 3
Mr. Rafiqueul Huq and Mr. M. Hafizullah, Amicus Curiae
parties:
Mostafa Kamal ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Commissioner of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque, J: Since the facts as well as the points of law are identical in both the writ petitions, we heard them together and we are disposing of the two cases by one judgment.

2. In both the cases Rules were issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders dated 23.10.96 and the impugned notification dated 18.9.96 vide Annexure-D and E respectively should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and of no legal effect and why the Respondents should not be directed to levy and collect customs duty. VAT and other taxes in respect of the said imported consignment on the basis of C & F value.

3. It is stated in the application that both the petitioners opened letter of credit on 26.8.96 for import of SODA ASH LIGHT under H.S. Code No. 2836.20 at the rate of US Doller 130 per metric ton. While those goods arrived at Chittagong port, the clearing agent of the petitioners submitted bill of entry with all the relevant papers and documents for clearing of the imported goods from the vessel on 23.10.96 on payment of customs duty. VA T and other charges as the basis of C & F Value at the rate of US Doller 130 per metric ton But the office of the Respondent No. 1 on 23.10.96 directed the petitioners to declare tariff value at US Doller 220 per metric ton on the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of customs duty and other charges in pursuance of SRO No. 2/96 Cus dated 18.9.96. It is alleged that tariff value as the aforesaid imported goods were assessed arbitrarily and as such the petitioners did not pay the customs duty on the tariff value which was fixed at US Doller 220 per metric ton. It is further submitted that tariff value would be assessed according to the value of the invoice and since the tariff value was fixed arbitrarily without considering the other circumstances the petitioners were not bound to pay the duty on the basis of tariff value at the rate of US Doller 220 per metric ton. It is further submitted that the tariff value was fixed under the provisions of section 25(7) of the Customs Act and this fixation of tariff value by notification dated 18.9.96 is absolutely arbitrary offending Articles 83.40 and 42 of the Constitution. As such the impugned notification is ultra vires of the Constitution.

4. Affidavit-in-opposition has been submitted on behalf of the Respondents. Further there are several supplementary affidavits and supplementary affidavits-in-opposition as well as reply in this case. We shall consider the papers whichever is necessary for the purpose of our judgment. It is stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioners opened L.C. on 26.3.96 and they were required to import the goods by 30.9.96. The L/C was revised on 3.10.96 and the petitioners were required to bring the goods by 30.10.96 Earlier the tariff value of such goods was fixed by notification dated 17.6.96 at U.S. Dollar 160 per metric ton. But by SRO dated 18.9.96 the tariff value was fixed at U.S. Dollar 220 per metric ton and according to this latest notification the tariff value was settled and the petitioners were required to pay duty on the basis of the tariff value fixed by notification dated 18.9.96. It is further stated that when the petitioners submitted the bill of entry with all other necessary papers, the tariff value stood 4t U.S. dollar 220 per metric ton and as such they are liable to pay the duty on the tariff value as per latest notification dated 18.9.96. In the affidavit-in-reply the petitions in fact, reiterated their statements as made in the writ petitioners. Further, some papers have been shown for importing of such goods by some other companies. Since there was discrimination in this matter, the Respondents were not authorised to fix the tariff value on the goods of the petitioners arbitrarily.

5. Before going into the merit of the case, the learned Attorney General appearing for the Respondent No. 4 has raised some preliminary objections. Learned Attorney General submits that since there was alternative remedy provided in the law itself namely, the Customs Act, the present applications are not maintainable. He further submits that already the petitioner filed applications before the Commissioner of Customs and without waiting for the result they hurriedly came before this court and obtained the present Rules. In such a situation, these writ petition are premature and the Rules are liable to be discharged. Learned Attorney General has referred to Section 193 of the Customs Act which shows the provisions of appeal as well as well the procedure for filing and disposal of the appeal.

6. Dr. Kamal Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that this preliminary objection cannot be entertained in view of the fad that section 193 must be read along with section 194 of the Customs Act. Section 194 of the Act shows that if duty is leviable then the entire amount of the leviable duty must be deposited first at the time of preferring the appeal and thereafter the appeal would be heard. Such a provision cannot be an efficacious remedy. He further submits that in the proviso to section 194 of the Act some provisions were made that in appropriate cases, the Commissioner may exempt the parties form paying the duties at the time of filing appeal Dr. Kamal Hossain submits that there is no guideline or any other rules as to within which time the Commissioner will consider the case and as to how this application will be disposed of. This will be a lengthy procedure in view of the fact that first there will be an application for exemption. If it is not allowed, then the petitioners will have to file appeal depositing the entire amount of duties leviable under the tariff value fixed by the authority. In such a case there will arise the question of demarrage for a long time as well as if the goods are perishable, the goods would be damaged. Since there is no time limit for disposing of the appeal and since this exemption of payment of duty is absolutely on the discretion of the Commissioner of Customs without rules or regulations, this provision of appeal cannot be an efficacious and adequate remedy.

7. Dr. Kamal Hossain further submits that since the petitioners have challenged the vires of the notification dated 18.9.96 itself, to file a writ petition before the High Court Division is an appropriate and efficacious remedy inasmuch as before the Commissioner of Customs the vires of the notification cannot be challenged and he has no authority to declare this notification illegal or void. We find full substance in the contention of Dr. Kamal Hossain. Considering the provisions of section 193 read with section 194 of the Customs Act and also considering the question that since the vires of the notification itself has been challenged in these two writ petitions to prefer the appeal before the Commissioner of Customs is not an efficacious and adequate remedy. As such the preliminary objections raised by the learned Attorney General are overruled.

8. Dr. Kamal Hossain submits that the impugned SRO was issued under the provisions of section 25(7) of the Customs Act which runs are follows:-

"Notwithstanding anything contained in this Section the Government may by notification in the official Gazette, fix, for the purpose of levying customs duties tariff values for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty ad-valorem."

9. Dr. Kamal Hossain submits that it is an excessive delegation of power to the executive authority without giving any guideline. Dr. Kamal Hossain submits that till today no rules or regulations have been framed by the authority although there are provisions for framing the rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act. Yet till today no rules giving any guidelines have been framed and as such this power of excessive delegation given under section 25(7) of the Customs Act is liable to be declared void being ultra vires of the Constitution vide Articles 83, 40 and 42 of the Constitution. In support of his submissions Dr. Kamal Hossain has referred to the cases of Hazi Ghuiam Zamir Vs. A.B. Khandker. 16 DIR 486: Dhaka -Picture Palace Vs. Pakistan 18DLR 442: Md. Hannan Vs. Collector of Customs, 40 DLR 273; M/S Yusuf Re-rolling Mills Vs. Collector of Customs. PLD 1989 (S.C.) 232 and M/S Devi Das Gopal Krishna Vs. The State of Punjab AIR1967 (S.C.) 1895. It appears that the principles enunciated in the above decisions are not disputed at all. But the thing which we are to consider here is that whether any guideline has been given in the act itself. Though admittedly no separate rules have been framed some of the rules of old law namely Sea Customer Act has been protected in the instant Customs Act. But it is relating to certain forms and procedures. With regard to the section 25(7) of the Act no rules or regulations have been framed by the Government.

10. In reply to this submission of Dr. Kamal Hossain learned Attorney General submits that we are to read section 25 of the Act as a whole along with other sections namely. Section 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. He submits that if we read the aforesaid provisions along with section 25(7) of the Act we will find that there are guidelines given by the legislature in the Act itself. Though no separate rule has been framed, yet the guideline given in the Act itself will be sufficient for the purpose of fixing tariff value of the imported goods.

11. Section 18 of Chapter V provides some provisions as to the goods dutiable. This section 18 is a charging section. Section 25 provides that the value of any imported goods shall be taken to be the normal price that is to say, the price which they would fetch, on the date referred to in section 30 on a sale in open marked between a buyer and a seller independent of each other. The normal price of any imported goods shall be determined on the assumptions which have been given in details in Section 25(2) and (3) of the Act. In this connection we are to read also section 30 of the Act. Section 30(1) provides that the value of and the rate of duty applicable to any imported goods shall be the value and the rate of duty in force the case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption under Section 79, on the date of which the bill of entry is presented under that section and in the case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption under section 104 on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse and in the case of any other goods on the date of payment of duty.

12. So, section 25 and 30 in fact, provide that the value of the imported goods would be fixed by the authority and the duty on the value would be paid according to tariff value which was in force on the day when the bill of entry along with other papers are presented to the authority. This has been clarified further when this Customs Act was amended by inserting section 30A in the Finance Act of the year 1995-96. The Parliament added Section 30A after section 30 and section 30A runs as follows:-

"Value and effective rate of duty -- Notwithstanding contained in another law for the time being in force or any decision of any court, for the purpose of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under sections, 18. 18A or 18B and the amount of duty that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or connection from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale of such goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof"

13. Lamed Attorney General submits that after insertion of this section 30A of the Finance Act of 1995-96 all doubts have been cleared off and this section 25(7) after the aforesaid amendment cannot be read independently inasmuch as since 1995 this section 25(7) must be read along with Section 25. 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. So, the other provisions, namely, Sections 25, 30 and 30A of the Act according to the learned Attorney General, are quite sufficient for giving guidelines in the matter of fixing of tariff value of the imported goods. He submits that section 30A of the Customs Act clearly shows that on the date of submission of the bill of entry after arrival of the goods the tariff value fixed on that day shall be the tariff value of the goods and the imported is bound to pay duty on the tariff value as given on the clay of submission of the bill of entry.

14. Mr. Rafiqul Huq and Mr. M. Hafizullah the two learned Senior Advocates of the Bar have assisted the Court as Amicus Curiae. It is their submissions that there are no separate rules or regulations with regard to fixation of tariff value on the imported goods. But it cannot be said that Act itself lacks totally the guideline in respect of fixing the tariff value of the goods. They submit that it is clear from Section 30(1) of the Act that when the bill of entry will be submitted before the authority, the tariff value fixed by the authority and prevalent or in existence on that day should be the basis of the tariff value and the importer shall have to pay duty on the tariff value fixed by the authority when bill of entry is presented. Learned Amicus-Curiae submit that the court can see the vires of law and the notification as well as arbitrariness of the decision of the authority. Though the non-obstante clause was with section 25(7) the other sections of the Customs Act, namely sections 25, 30 and 30A of the Act should be read as a whole along with the non-obstante clause of 25(7). It is submitted by them that though separate rules or regulations have not been framed under section 25(7) of the Act, it cannot be declared unconstitutional for want of any guideline in view of the fact that in fact the other sections namely sections 25, 30 and 30A of the Act have given guideline for fixation of the tariff value of the imported goods. Since some guidelines have been given the court can see only the arbitrariness of the decision of the authority. If the materials are there for fixing the tariff value of the imported goods by the authority concerned and if the authority concerned considered other materials as required under law and fixed the tariff value, this Court cannot see the sufficiency or insufficiency of the materials for taking decision by the authority. But the learned Amicus Curiae submits that if it appears that such tariff value has been fixed arbitrarily whimsically and capriciously by the authority without any materials, definitely this court has got jurisdiction to look into the matter and strike down the decision of the authority.

15. In this connection the learned Advocate for respondents which No. 3 Mr. Zakir Ahmed has placed before us certain materials which are annexed to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 26.11.96 on behalf of the Respondents. In this supplementary affidavit-in-opposition the learned Advocate has annexed a document vide Annexure-4 which shows the fixation of tariff value/re-fixation of tariff value and re-examination of the tariff value by a high power advisory committee constituted by the Finance Ministry vide File No. 2(63) Shulko-5/92/497-503 dated 28.7.94 and it was the duty of that committee to re-consider and re-examine the tariff value of the imported goods within every three months. This Annexure-4 shows that a meeting of the high powers committee was held on 21st of August, 1996 in order to re-consider and re-fixation of the tariff value of the imported goods. The committee was constituted by the Finance Minister on 28.7.94. In this committee the representatives of the National Board of Revenue, the Tariff Fixation Department, Ministry of Commerce Ministry of Industries Ministry of Textile, Tariff Commission, Commissioners, Customs House Chittagong and Dhaka and Member of Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industries, are the members. This high powered committee held a meeting on 21st August. 1996 and in that meeting they considered the question of fixation of tariff value of the imported goods including the goods in question. According to the suggestion of this committee the tariff value of some imported goods were kept intact, sonic were reduced and some were enhanced. So, it appears that though the separate rules and regulations have not been framed yet the authority can fix tip tariff value according to section 25(7) of the Act and it appears that on 28.7.94 the high powered Advisory Committee consisting of the representatives of different Ministries and the concerned authorities had been constituted by the Finance Ministry and they held meetings within every three months in order to consider the re-fixation of tariff value of the imported goods. According to the decision of the high powered committee dated 21.8.96 this notification dated 18.9.96 was issued where in the tariff value of the goods in question have been fixed at US dollar 220 per metric ton.

16. Mr. Zakir Ahmed has also referred to Annexure-5 of the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition which is the summary prepared by the Secretary of the Ministry of Finance. This summary Annexure-5 shows that in 31 items the committee suggested for reduction of tariff value and in 10 items including Soda Ash the committee suggested for enhancement of tariff value. The Secretary of the Ministry of Finance also considered the matter in details and thereafter he placed it before the Hon'ble Ministry for approval. It was prepared on 5.9.96 and approved by the Finance Minister on 14.9.96. Thereafter on 18.9.96 the notification was made for enhancement of tariff value on the goods of the present petitioners at US dollar 220 per metric ton.

17. In these cases the letters of credit were opened on 26.8.96. By previous SRO dated 17.6.96 the tariff value of the Soda Ash was fixed at U.S. Dollar 160 per metric ton. High powers committee's meeting was held on 21.8.96 and the decision of the high powered committee was placed before the Secretary. Ministry of Finance. The Secretary, Ministry of Finance, in details considered the matter in question along with other matters for fixation of tariff value and thereafter on 5.9.96 he placed it before the Finance Minister who approved the same on 14.9.96 and according to the suggestions of this high powered committee the tariff value of the goods in question was fixed at U.S. Dollar 220 per metric ton. In this view of the matter, it appears to us that fixation of tariff value at US dollar 220 per metric ton instead of US dollar 130 cannot be called an arbitrary decision of the Government. Though there are no specific Rules and Regulations yet if we read section 25(7) along with Sections, 25, 30 and 30A of the Act, it appears to us that there are guidelines given in the Act for fixation of tariff value and actually the legislature has given power to the authority to consider the case and fix the tariff value of the imported goods. Here, this question of arbitrariness may arise in view of the fact that since there was no specific Rules, the authority can arbitrarily fix the tariff value of the imported goods. But, since it appears that in 1994 the high powered advisory committee was constituted in every .three months this high powered committee used to sit and consider the question of fixing tariff value of imported goods and since the high powered committee was constituted with the representatives of the different Ministries, relevant agencies of the Government and business organisations, we are of the view that the fixation of tariff value at U.S. Dollar 220 per metric ton cannot be called illegal and arbitrary. As the high powered committee considered the matter, this court is not in a position to consider the validity or invalidity, sufficiency or insufficiency of the decision of the high powered committee in view of the fact that the committee was constituted by the Government with the representatives of the Board or Revenue several Ministries and other relevant authorities and organisations. It is desirable that in order to resolve this problem once for all, some rules and regulations should be framed by the Government so that such dispute may not arise in future. Section 219 of the Customs Act provides that the Board may by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

18. As Section 25(7) of the Act has given the authority to fix the tariff value advalorem and as no specific rule has been framed showing the procedure as to how the tariff value is to be fixed, it is desired by this court that the National Board of Revenue should frame rules with regard to the provision of section 25(7) of the Act in order to avoid all complications. Further, it will clear all the misunderstandings as to the fixing up tariff value as well as the duty payable on the tariff value.

19. Since it appears to us that sections 25, 30 and 30A of the Act, in fact, have given some guidelines as to the fact that on the dated of submitting the bill of entry before the authority along with other papers and documents the tariff value of the imported goods in existence will be taken as the value of the goods for duty and such value of the goods is fixed by the Government according to the suggestions of the high powered committee. Further, it shows that the tariff value of the imported goods shall be fixed in the way referred to in section 30 on a sale of the goods in open market between a buyer and seller independent of each other.

<u>20. This is an important provisions in view of the fact that as to what would be the value of the goods in open market between the buyers and the sellers will be decided by the authority. Since in the instant case it appears that before submission of the bill of entry before the authority the high powered committee considered the matter and suggested for enhancement of tariff value of the goods in question at U.S. Dollar 220 per metric ton, it cannot be said that it was fixed arbitrarily and the notification as well as the law itself are ultra vires of the Constitution on the point of excessive delegation without having any guideline. Since the notification was issued as per the decision of the high powered committee which considered the matter according to the provisions of sections 25, 30 and 30A of the Customs Act, we are of the view that the impugned notification or the law itself, that is. Section 25(7) of the Customs Act cannot be declared ultra vires or to have been made and passed without any lawful authority. In view of the above, we find that the tariff value fixed by the impugned notification has been done in accordance with the law and as such this court does not find any reason to interfere with the impugned notification issued by the Respondents.</u>

21. We take note of the valuable assistance rendered by the two learned Amicus Curiae with deep appreciation.

22. In the result, these two Rules are discharged without any order as to cost and the impugned notification and orders are found valid.

23. Let a Copy of the judgment be sent to the Secretary Ministry of Finance. Government of Bangladesh for consideration of framing Rules.

24. The certificate prayed for under Article 103 of the Constitution is refused.

End.
